tip: Στην ώρα μας (stin óra mas) = on time – literally 'at our hour'.
Φοβάμαι (fováme) = I'm afraid of – the thing feared follows straight after, as in τα αεροπλάνα (ta aeropléna), with no 'of' word.
Φοβήθηκα (fovíthika) = I got scared, one specific fright – the one-time past of φοβάμαι (fováme = I'm afraid). Greek splits one-off events from ongoing states in the verb itself.
Το χθεσινό (to khthesinó) = yesterday's thing – an adjective doing a noun's job.
Ο μικρός (o mikrós) = the little one – 'the' plus an adjective, with the noun left out.
Μου έλειψες (mu élipses) = I missed you – literally 'you were missing to me'.
Δεν νομίζω (dhen nomízo) = I don't think so – Greek needs no word for 'so'.
Το πιστεύω αυτό (to pistévo aftó) = I believe that – the little το (to) sits before the verb.
Έχω δίκιο (ékho díkio) = to be right, literally 'to have right'; here έχεις (ékhis) makes it 'you are right'.
Κάνω λάθος (káno láthos) = to be wrong, literally 'to make a mistake': κάνεις λάθος (kánis láthos) = you're wrong.
Ας (as) plus a verb = let's: ας μη μαλώνουμε (as mi malónume) = let's not fight. For the negative, μη (mi) slots straight in after ας.
Ένα δίκιο (éna díkio) = a point – the ένα (éna = a) turns 'you're right' into partial agreement.
The liked thing is the subject, so plural things flip the verb: μου αρέσουν τα βίντεο (mu arésun ta vídeo) = the videos please me. One thing would take αρέσει (arési).
A να (na) clause counts as one single thing, so it takes αρέσει (arési), not αρέσουν (arésun): μας αρέσει να ταξιδεύουμε (mas arési na taksidhévume) = traveling pleases us.
Past plural: μου άρεσαν (mu áresan) = I liked them.
When the liker is a full word rather than μου/σου, σε (se) marks them: άρεσε σε όλους (árese se ólus) = it pleased everyone. The food stays the subject.
Μου αρέσει που γελάς (mu arési pu yelás) = I like that you laugh – που (pu) points at a real fact. Να (na) instead would mean liking the idea of laughing in general.
Πάμε Κρήτη (páme Kríti) = we're going to Crete – in casual speech place names often drop the 'to the'.
Σίγουρη (síghuri) is the form used for a woman; for a man it's σίγουρος (síghuros) – the word for sure matches the person.
Τι (ti) plus an adjective = what a: τι ωραία! (ti oréa) = how lovely! – no verb needed.
Μπράβο σου (brávo su) = good for you – μπράβο pairs with σου (su = to you), or σας (sas) for a group.
Τι λες! (ti les) = no way! – literally 'what are you saying'.
Επιτέλους (epitélus) = finally – it carries relief, not just 'in the end'.
Τι μέρα κι αυτή (ti méra ki aftí) = what a day – the κι αυτή (ki aftí) tag adds an exasperated tone.
Στενοχωρημένη (stenokhoriméni) = upset – the -μένος/-μένη (-ménos/-méni) ending describes the state someone is in.
Δεν έγινε τίποτα (dhen éyine típota) = literally 'nothing happened', the everyday way to say no harm done.
Φοβόμουν (fovómun) = I used to be afraid – the ongoing past, for a fear that lasted a while.
Λυπητερό (lipiteró) = sad, for things like a movie's τέλος (télos = ending). Sad people are λυπημένοι (lipiméni) – Greek splits what causes sadness from who feels it.
Γελάσαμε (yelásame) = we laughed, and what you laugh at takes με (me = with): με τα αστεία (me ta astía) = at the jokes.
Πιο (pio) plus an adjective = more: πιο φωτεινό (pio fotinó) = brighter, with no ending change.
